title: Washing and shrouds
hook: the body is washed and dressed in plain white shrouds, the same for everyone

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was chevra kadisha, and your line was the holy society: true kindness that can't be repaid. What did you do that no one will know about? Today, what the holy society actually does. Day one thousand three hundred eighteen.

Families were running away from their own dead. That's the scene the Talmud describes. Burial had become so expensive, with fine clothes and costly display, that for some, the cost of a funeral was harder to bear than the death itself. Some relatives would leave the body and flee. Then Rabban Gamliel, a leader of his generation, made a request about his own funeral: bury me in plain linen. And the people followed him, and carried out their own dead in linen too. Today's word is the washing that comes before that plain linen.
screen: `FAMILIES FLED THEIR DEAD.` → `BURY ME IN PLAIN LINEN.` → `THE PEOPLE FOLLOWED.`

segments.voice: Tahara. Purification. It is the ritual washing of the body before burial, done by the holy society. Turn it four ways. First, the washing. The body is cleaned gently and thoroughly, with the face kept covered and only the part being washed uncovered, out of modesty. Then water is poured over the whole body in a continuous flow. Members of the society say verses and prayers as they work, and in some communities, at the end, they say the words: tehorah hi, she is pure, or tahor hu, he is pure. Second, the shrouds. They're called tachrichim. Plain white garments, usually linen or cotton, sewn by hand, with no pockets, and in some traditions no buttons or knots. A Yiddish saying goes: shrouds have no pockets. You take nothing with you. Third, the same for everyone. A rabbi and a cab driver, a philanthropist and a person who died with nothing: dressed alike. That goes back to Rabban Gamliel's plain linen. Equality in death was not an accident; it was a decision, made so no family would be shamed. Some men are also wrapped in their own tallit, the prayer shawl, with one fringe cut. Fourth, the echo. In the book of Job, after losing everything, Job says: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither." Tahara treats the body almost the way a newborn is treated: washed by others, wrapped by others, held by others. Everyone equal in death.
screen: `WASHED WITH MODESTY.` · `PLAIN WHITE SHROUDS, NO POCKETS.` · `RABBI AND CAB DRIVER, ALIKE.` · `NAKED CAME I.` · then, large: `EVERYONE EQUAL IN DEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wear something plain. Before the sit, or right after, look at what you're wearing. Settle, and breathe. Notice what in it says something about you: a brand, a ring, a badge, a style. Without judging any of it, ask: if all of this were taken off and replaced with one plain white garment, what would still be me? Let the answer be whatever it is. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can say the line from Job slowly, or sit in silence. The bell holds the time.
Tahara. Purification: the washing of the body, the flow of water, and plain white shrouds, the same for everyone. Today's word.
Your line: everyone equal in death. Today, wear something plain, and treat the most important person you meet exactly like the least. Day one thousand three hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Before a traditional Jewish burial, members of the chevra kadisha perform tahara, washing the body with care and pouring water over it, then dress it in simple white shrouds called tachrichim; some men are also wrapped in their tallit.

options: ask to be buried in plain linen yourself.
pay for every funeral from the treasury.
fork.reveal: he asked for plain linen at his own burial, and the people followed him.

original.note: Hebrew: purification, the washing before burial.

trapdoor: what you thought: the body is cleaned the way any funeral home would.
what it means: a ritual washing with prayer and modesty, then plain white shrouds for everyone.
what a scholar hears: Moed Katan 27b and Ketubot 8b on Rabban Gamliel's linen, which made equal burial a deliberate choice.

notes: Job 1:21 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.
Rabban Gamliel story (Moed Katan 27b; Ketubot 8b) paraphrased; confirm the 'families fled' detail and 'the people followed'.
Tahara procedure (modesty, continuous pouring, 'tehorah hi / tahor hu') described generally; customs vary. Confirm.
Shrouds 'no pockets, no buttons or knots in some traditions' and the Yiddish saying 'shrouds have no pockets' — confirm.
'Some men are also wrapped in their tallit, with one fringe cut' — customs vary; confirm.
Hook calls Rabban Gamliel 'a leader of his generation' — kept general; confirm.

Editor: replaced the hook's unsourced 'the poor stopped being shamed, and the rich stopped competing' with what Ketubot 8b says (the people followed him and were carried out in linen); untangled the shrouds sentence so 'in some traditions' applies only to buttons and knots.
